text:
REALLY late to the show...
2022, and I was in the situation where my PC was randomly losing all i/o, (USB and video), so I needed a rebuild. I also wanted to stick with Win7, as I have had nothing but HORRIBLE experiences with Win10 updates trashing systems; however, the AMD 5000 series was the last series AMD really supported with drivers and PCIEv3.
In April 2022, I think I bought the last "new" (not even ex-display), RX 5600XTs in the UK; an MSI Mech OC model, one of the worst rated models out there (this HAS the revised AMD BIOS increasing RAM speed etc).

Out of the box it was fairly hot and noisy, just like many of the reviews, so I started messing with settings to try and tame the fan noise; long story short - lowering the fan speeds also REDUCED the heat; after experimenting, I am now running the fans at around 30%, making it a lot quieter, and the temps are around 70C UNDER FULL LOAD.

In other words, dont assume higher fan RPM equals better cooling; MSI have really screwed up the cooling solution on this model.

One caveat, I have an EATX case with excellent airflow, 3 low speed fans pulling air in from the front, back (CPU AIO), and bottom; and two low speed fans pushing air out of the top (all fans around 940RPM max).

AMD low and mid-range 6000 series cards are fucked up for people without PCIEv4, as they use 8, or even FOUR PCI lanes, instead of 16; yet the cards are supposed to be aimed at budget buyers who probably HAVE older PCIEv3 motherboards.

The Sapphire 5500XT was only $20 cheaper for 30% less FPS performance while the Sapphire 5700XT was $170 more for only 10% better performance.

text:
@markhamil3916  You're correct that they could save money, but I don't think they should change much about their system. (Sorry for the long comment btw!)

Here's why I think that, a 600W PSU does two things for Monica, 1, it puts the power consumption right at the peak of the efficiency curve, saving money on their power bill over time, and 2, gives the option to upgrade later to a far more powerful CPU+GPU without risk, besides, the cost difference between a 500W and a 600W PSU of equivalent quality is not enough to save up for a 5700XT.

The cost difference between m.2 and SATA is roughly 10 quid at this point, which isn't enough to step up the GPU unless you drop the capacity, sure there are faster m.2 drives, but the better drives cost a lot more, so why not get the P1?

That motherboard is excellent and will last a very long time through a decent number of upgrades, sacrificing motherboard VRM quality to save a few quid isn't worth it, anything below about 90 quid is crud, so saving 30 quid there still won't step up the GPU, and even if they did all of those, you'd save maybe 70 quid.

A cheaper case might push that to 100 quid, but that would only get the cheapest, shittiest RX5700XT, which will be hot, loud and poorly made.

If they had chosen vastly overpriced parts I'd happily recommend changing things for better value parts, but they've clearly done their homework and I'd be happy to put my name to a build of that quality.

Saving now means spending later, so buying good quality stuff that is reliable and has upgrade options is a smarter move than buying bottom tier guff to save money, besides, the parts they chose can always be sold on to recoup those costs when the time to upgrade comes, and those parts will hold their value better than cheaper ones.
